lesson.title: Integer programming and branch and bound

scenes.narration: A model for the field-trip budget tells the faculty to hire two and a half buses. Rounding up breaks the budget, and rounding down leaves students behind. What should the model have said?

scenes.on_screen_text: Integer programming and branch and bound
scenes.narration: Today: why many real decisions need whole numbers, why rounding a linear solution can fail badly, and how branch and bound finds proven optima.
An integer program is a linear program in which some variables must be whole numbers. Yes-or-no decisions become zero-one variables. This small change makes the problem far harder in general.

In the knapsack problem, each item has a weight and a value, and we choose items to maximise value within a capacity. The linear relaxation allows fractions of items. Its value is an upper bound on the true optimum.

Here the relaxation happens to be whole, giving sixteen. But change the capacity to seven, and the relaxation picks a and two thirds of c, worth fourteen. Rounding down gives ten, yet b plus c gives thirteen.

Branch and bound splits on a fractional variable, solving one branch with it set to zero and one with it set to one. Each relaxation gives a bound. Any branch whose bound is worse than the best whole solution found so far is pruned.

scenes.on_screen_text: Teach with a tree on the board
scenes.narration: Students tend to round linear solutions or believe the solver checks every combination. Draw the branch-and-bound tree for a four-item knapsack on the board. Let students compute each bound and decide which branches to prune.
Quick check! The relaxation of a maximisation knapsack gives fourteen. What does that tell you about the integer optimum?
It is at most fourteen. The relaxation has more freedom, so it can only do as well or better. Here the true optimum is thirteen.
In the app, open the knapsack lab. Pick items by hand, compare with the relaxation, and watch branch and bound prune its tree.
Your turn. The best whole solution so far is thirteen. A branch's relaxation gives twelve. What should branch and bound do?
Prune it: nothing in that branch can beat thirteen. Remember: relaxations give bounds, rounding can be far from optimal, and branch and bound proves optimality by pruning.

scenes.on_screen_text: Try it in your next lecture
scenes.narration: Try it in your next lecture: give pairs a four-item knapsack and ask them to round the relaxation first. Then draw the branch-and-bound tree together. Compare the rounded answer with the proven optimum.

checkpoints.prompt: A maximisation relaxation gives 14. The integer optimum is:
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: the relaxation is an upper bound.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: allowing fractions can only help a maximisation, so it bounds from above.

checkpoints.prompt: Best whole solution 13; a branch's relaxation gives 12. What next?
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: its bound is below the incumbent, so nothing inside can win.
